messages.content: What are the different properties of Hydrogen?

message.content:
**Hydrogen (H)** – the simplest and most abundant element in the universe – has a rich set of physical, chemical, and nuclear properties that make it unique among the elements. Below is a concise overview of its key characteristics:

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Symbol | H |
| | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u (protium dominates) |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | Protium (¹H), Deuterium (²H), Tritium (³H) |
| | Natural abundance | 99.98 % ¹H, 0.02 % ²H, trace ³H |
| **Physical Properties** | State at STP | Gas |
| | Boiling point | –252.9 °C (20.3 K) |
| | Melting point | –259.2 °C (14.0 K) |
| | Density (at 0 °C, 1 atm) | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume (ideal gas) | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Specific heat capacity (gas, 25 °C) | 28.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Thermal conductivity | ~0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 300 K) |
| | Refractive index (visible light) | ~1.00013 |
| | Solubility in water | ~1.6 × 10⁻³ M (≈0.18 g L⁻¹) |
| **Chemical Properties** | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | First ionization energy | 1312 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Electron affinity | –73 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Oxidation states | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride) |
| | Bond dissociation energy (H–H) | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | pKa of hydronium (H₃O⁺) | –1.7 (strong acid) |
| | Standard enthalpy of formation (gas) | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ (by definition) |
| | Standard entropy (gas) | 130.68 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Standard Gibbs free energy of formation (gas) | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Flammability | Extremely flammable; explosive limits: 4–75 % (v/v) in air |
| | Combustion reaction | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (ΔH° ≈ –286 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Acid–base behavior | Acts as a weak base when forming hydrides (e.g., NaH) |
| | Redox behavior | Can act as both reducing agent (e.g., in metal hydrides) and oxidizing agent (in high‑pressure environments) |
| **Nuclear Properties** | Nuclear spin (protium) | ½ |
| | Magnetic moment (protium) | 2.792847 µ_N |
| | Half‑life of tritium | 12.32 years |
| | Decay mode of tritium | β⁻ decay to helium‑3 |
| **Applications & Uses** | Energy carrier | Fuel cells (electrolyzers produce H₂ from water) |
| | Rocket propellant | Liquid hydrogen + liquid oxygen (LH₂/LOX) |
| | Metallurgy | Reducing agent for metal extraction (e.g., iron from ore) |
| | Chemical synthesis | Feedstock for ammonia (NH₃) via Haber process |
| | Medical imaging | Deuterated compounds used in NMR/MRI contrast agents |
| | Fusion research | Deuterium–tritium fusion experiments (ITER, tokamaks) |
| | Food industry | Hydrogenation of fats/oils (producing margarine, shortening) |
| | Semiconductor manufacturing | Plasma etching, doping processes |
| | Environmental science | Indicator of microbial activity (methanogenesis) |

### Quick Takeaways

- **Lightest element**: Hydrogen’s low mass makes it ideal for propulsion and energy storage.
- **Highly reactive**: Forms a wide variety of compounds (e.g., acids, amides, organometallics).
- **Isotopic diversity**: Deuterium and tritium have distinct nuclear properties useful in spectroscopy and fusion.
- **Energy potential**: Clean fuel source when produced via electrolysis powered by renewables.

Feel free to ask for deeper details on any specific property or application!
